summary: Defines a Sieve extension for comparing the user and detail parts of addresses that use subaddressing, such as ken+sieve@example.org. It replaces RFC 3598. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Some addresses have a tag after a plus sign. This lets mail rules look at the tag by itself, so tagged mail can be sorted.

questions: what is the sieve subaddress extension
how to filter plus addressing in sieve
subtitle: Lets Sieve mail filters look at the user and detail parts of addresses like ken+sieve@example.org.

tldr.problem: Some mail systems let people add 'detail' to an address, as in ken+sieve@example.org, but the base Sieve language cannot compare against just the user part or just the detail part.
tldr.mechanism: The subaddress extension adds two address parts, :user and :detail, that can be used with the address and envelope tests to pick out those sub-parts of the local-part.
tldr.outcome: A script can file mail by the detail tag, such as sending list mail addressed to ken+mta-filters into its own mailbox. It is a Proposed Standard that replaces RFC 3598.

today: RFC 5233 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2008. It obsoletes RFC 3598 and is not itself marked as obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Subaddressing
sections.content:
Subaddressing means adding 'detail' information to the local-part of an RFC 2822 address to give the address extra meaning. A common way is a separator character sequence such as + that divides the 'user' (the original local-part) from the 'detail', much as @ divides the local-part from the domain.

The RFC gives two typical uses. A message sent to ken+sieve@example.org goes into a mailbox called sieve belonging to user ken. A message sent to 5551212#123@example.com goes to voice mailbox 123 at phone number 5551212.

This document extends the Sieve language of RFC 5228 so scripts can compare against the user and detail sub-parts. Its capability string is subaddress.
sections.eli5: Think of a street address with an apartment number. The part before the plus is the person, and the part after is like the apartment number saying where in their mail to put it.

sections.title: The :user and :detail Address Parts
sections.content:
Test commands that act only on addresses may take the optional tagged arguments :user and :detail. They choose which sub-part of the local-part is tested. They are added to the ADDRESS-PART syntax element of RFC 5228, and follow the same rules as the standard address parts.

  • :user is the user sub-part. If the address has no detail encoded, it is the entire left side of the address, the same as :localpart.
  • :detail is the detail sub-part. If the address has no detail encoded, the address fails to match any of the keys. If a zero-length string is encoded as the detail, :detail is the empty value.
sections.eli5: You can ask the rule to look at just the name part or just the tag part. If there is no tag, asking for the tag finds nothing.

sections.title: Where the Detail Goes
sections.content:
The RFC shows two layouts. With a detail that follows +, the local-part is :user, then +, then :detail. With a detail that precedes --, the order is reversed: :detail, then --, then :user. In both layouts the domain follows @.

The encoding is specific to the site or implementation. Implementations MUST make sure the encoding they assume matches the one used or allowed by the mail system around them, or results may be unexpected. How a system defines or reports its encoding is outside the scope of the RFC. If the separator occurs more than once, how the address is split is implementation-defined.
sections.eli5: Different mail systems put the tag in different places and use different separator marks. The filter has to know which one the mail system uses.

sections.title: Which Address to Examine
sections.content:
The RFC notes that in most cases the envelope to address is the best one to examine for subaddress information when sorting by how a message was addressed to reach a specific recipient. That address is the reason the message is being processed by the script for that user. It matters most with mailing lists, aliases and virtual domains, where the envelope may be the only source of the detail for that recipient.

Using the extension on foreign addresses, such as the envelope from address or originator header fields, may give inconsistent or incorrect results, because the encoding of detailed addresses is site or implementation specific.
sections.eli5: Look at the address the mail was actually delivered to, because that is the one that has your tag. Other people's addresses might use tags in their own way.

sections.title: Example Script
sections.content:
The RFC's example assumes one user account that receives mail for both ken@example.com and postmaster@example.com. It requires envelope, subaddress and fileinto, and does three things.

  • Anything sent to postmaster (tested with :user) goes to inbox.postmaster, then the script stops.
  • Mail whose :detail is mta-filters, the way the mailing list was subscribed, goes to inbox.ietf-mta-filters.
  • Mail whose :detail is foo is redirected to ken@example.net.
sections.eli5: The example is a sorting robot: mail for the postmaster goes in one box, mail tagged for the mailing list goes in another, and mail tagged foo gets forwarded.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC points to the security considerations of RFC 5228 and says it is believed that this extension does not introduce any additional security concerns.
sections.eli5: Looking at the tag on an address does not open any new doors for bad guys, as far as the authors can tell.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 3598
sections.content: The discussion of how user and detail information is encoded now uses generic language. New notes say the extension is most useful on the envelope to address and not very useful on foreign addresses. The envelope example now uses only the to address, and the :user example was replaced with one that does not produce unexpected behavior. The zero-length string is now called 'empty' rather than 'null', following RFC 5228, and examples use only RFC 2606 domains.
sections.eli5: This second edition explains things more clearly and fixes examples that could confuse people.
